title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission
location: DNCR , 308
description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.

The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.

Commission meetings are held quarterly to review applications and discuss Certification policies and procedures.

The commission's meeting dates for the 2025-2026 year are October 27, 2025, January 9, 2026, April 10, 2026, and July 10, 2026. All meetings are held at the Library of NC beginning at 1:00 pm unless otherwise posted. Information about meetings can be found on the North Carolina Secretary of State's meeting calendar.

Have questions about certification? Contact us at NC.Certification.Commission@dncr.nc.gov.

title: IAH Fellows Forum: Antonia Randolph
location: Hyde Hall, University Room
description:
On Oct. 30, American studies Assistant Professor Antonia Randolph (FFP ’22) will give a Fellows Forum presentation titled “It’s All Love? Beyoncé and Jay-Z and the Re-enchantment of Black Romance in the Age of the Manosphere.”

 

This talk will examine Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s post-2010 output, with an emphasis on Everything Is Love (The Carters, 2018) and Renaissance (Beyoncé, 2022), to show how their defense of romantic love converts their need to salvage their brand as hip-hop and R&B’s happily married power couple into a story about saving the Black nation through heteronormative marriage.

 

To satisfy R&B audiences, they infuse their marriage with Black nationalist significance, with its survival serving as a proxy for the survival of the Black nation. They link social mobility and wealth with heteronormative marriage, simultaneously turning marriage into an aspirational luxury item while encouraging people to look to marriage, rather than the state, to escape poverty.

 

At the same time, they satisfy hip-hop’s norms by constructing Beyoncé as uniquely deserving of empathy as the ultimate “ride or die” chick, denying that other Black women deserve the care and consideration she receives. These individualized, anti-redistributive responses to shifting gender norms and the erosion of the social safety net in the post-Civil Rights Era provide a cultural commonsense that supports the Black manosphere.

 

Antonia Randolph is the Jonathan M. Hess Career Development Term Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Her interests include diversity discourse in education, Black feminist thought, non-normative Black masculinity and sexuality, and hip-hop culture. Her book, The Wrong Kind of Different: Challenging the Meaning of Diversity in American Classrooms (Teachers College Press, 2012), examined the hierarchies elementary school teachers constructed among students of color. Her current book project, That’s My Heart: Queering Intimacy in Hip-Hop Culture, forthcoming from the University of California Press, examines portrayals of Black men’s intimate relationships in hip-hop culture.

title: "Black Lodge" and "Bardo"
location: Memorial Hall
description:
The night before Halloween, Memorial Hall transforms into something unsettling and mysterious. 

 

Before the performance even begins, audiences are invited to enter BARDO, a haunting, liminal place between death and rebirth. Come dressed in your Halloween finest and venture through spaces rarely open to audiences. Eerie installations. Strange encounters. Unsettling imagery. Around every corner, the sense that something is waiting—and watching—just out of sight. North Carolina performers bring this dreamscape to life to create an experience that haunts long after the night is over. 

 

The journey culminates with BLACK LODGE, a dark Lynchian goth-rock opera about a tormented writer trapped in the nightmarish Bardo, where he is forced to confront the darkest moment of his life again and again. Through the blending of music, theater, and film, the performance explores what it means to reckon with the worst thing you have ever done. Together, the two experiences create an evening that feels less like attending a traditional performance and more like stepping into a collective late-night fever dream. Enter if you dare. 

 

*This two-part event begins with BARDO at 7 p.m., followed by BLACK LODGE at 9 p.m. A single ticket includes both experiences.

 

*Get in on the spirit of horror movies and Halloween – audience members are encouraged to arrive in costume!

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/blacklodgeandbardo/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Play the Cyber Bowl
description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy. 

 

All October long, students, faculty and staff can log into the Cyber Bowl website and take a short cybersecurity quiz. Each completed quiz earns a point for Carolina.

 

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. In the inaugural Cyber Bowl, Carolina won the championship by garnering the largest participation by percentage. Last year, Carolina fielded the most players — almost 2,000 — of any school.

 

The Cyber Bowl is sponsored by Information Technology Services and the Information Security Office as part of National Cybersecurity Awareness Month.

title: Batty Bio Blitz
location: Visitor Center
description: Bats are often misunderstood because of their association with Halloween and all things spooky - from their leathery wings to their cave-like habitats. Come visit our Batty Bio Blitz display at the Visitor Center to discover more about bat ecology, their unique adaptations, the important roles they play in our ecosystems, and how we can help conserve and protect these remarkable animals. title: Botanizing at Occoneechee Mountain
location: Occoneechee Mountain
description:
This North Carolina State Natural Area is a gem, with a diversity of natural plant and animal communities not found anywhere else in the Triangle region. Join Paul Manos, Duke biology professor and Duke Herbarium curator, and Alec Motten, professor emeritus, Duke University Department of Biology, on a two- to three-mile mountain hike of moderate difficulty. Both Alec and Paul bring a deep expertise in plants and ecology; they will “read” the landscape and give you a unique view of Occoneechee Mountain. Please wear comfortable clothes and good walking shoes. Bring a lunch and beverage to enjoy and continue the conversation after the hike. 
Fee: $38; 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Free parking available. 
Location: Occoneechee Mountain. Driving directions will be sent with the reminder for participants to meet at the site. 
Accessibility: This will be a small group program that takes place outdoors traveling on unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and steep inclines. This walk includes a ~400’ elevation gain from the Eno River to the viewpoint.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Death and Mourning in the Mountains: A Special Guided Tour at Vance Birthplace
location: Governor Zebulon B. Vance Birthplace
description:
Join us at Vance Birthplace on Saturday, Oct. 31 for our new Death and Mourning in the Mountains tour to learn how the culture around death and funerary practices changed throughout the 1800s. Led by site staff, you’ll move through the historic grounds to explore how the Appalachian climate and cultures of Western North Carolina as well as technological advances in the funeral industry shaped the end of life in the mountains.

Tours are offered at 10am and 1pm and will last approximately 90 minutes, including an optional hike to the old Vance family cemetery. Tickets cost $10.70 per person via Zeffy. Spots are limited, so we recommend registering in advance. Join us to learn, ask questions, and connect with the region’s history through this rarely discussed chapter of Appalachian history.

If you have any questions, please feel free to reach out to us at vance@dncr.nc.gov or give us a call at (828) 645-6706!

location: 5 Points Gallery, 109 E Chapel Hill St, Durham, NC, 27701, United States
description:

Grounded in Blazing’s experiences of Carolina, the layered works draw from travel, accumulated visual memories, and unexpected connections that emerge as the paintings evolve to create landscapes that feel familiar without belonging to any single geography. Throughout the gallery, visitors can also enjoy work by our ten Triangle-based artists, offering a refreshing mix of painting, sculpture, fused glass, mixed media, and finely crafted furniture, with each artist bringing a distinct creative perspective. title: Open Studio: Glass & Other
location: Fusion Gallery, 321 W Main St, Durham, 27701, United States
description:
Open Studio Day Pass
Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM. 
Use our studio space and tools or bring your own project to work on—perfect for artists who don’t have a home studio or simply want dedicated time and space to make. Personal cubbies are also available to store works-in-progress between visits. 
Online registration or sign-up via email is required before coming in. Drop-ins are not permitted at this time. If you’d like to come in at a time you don’t see available online, email us at info@fusionnc.com. 
How Open Studio Works
Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction. You should already have the skills needed to safely work in your chosen medium. It’s also a great opportunity to finish projects started during a Fusion class. 
Your Day Pass includes access to our shared workspace, tools, equipment, and currently available non-consumable materials. Consumable and specialty materials are charged separately based on usage. 
Stained & Fused Glass
Prior stained or fused glass experience is required to use our glass tools. Taking a basics or beginner class at Fusion is recommended, but previous instruction at Carolina Stained Glass or Say It With Glass is also accepted. 
• Glass, solder, foil, and frit: $35/lb
• Bringing your own stained glass? Foil and solder use: $6
• Paper stained glass patterns: Free
• Vinyl-cut patterns: $3 each
• An assortment of stained glass patterns is available for studio use
• Kiln firings are handled by Fusion staff only 
Silver Clay
Prior silver clay experience is required to use silver clay tools. Taking a beginner class at Fusion is recommended before using the studio independently. 
• Silver clay: $7/gram prior to firing
• Firing of your completed piece is included and will be completed at the convenience of Fusion studio staff
• Guests may not fire their own pieces without prior authorization from Fusion’s owners 
Drawing & Painting
No prior class or experience is required for drawing or painting. Your Open Studio fee includes access to currently available shared drawing and painting materials. 
Please Note
• Day Pass access is valid 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected date only
• Online or email registration is required before arriving—no walk-ins
• Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction
• Some specialty tools, equipment, or processes may require prior approval or demonstrated experience
• Guests are responsible for cleaning their workspace and helping maintain a respectful shared environment
• Misuse of the space, tools, or equipment or failure to follow studio guidelines may result in removal from the studio without refund

DURHAM, NC — Sleepy Cat Records will celebrate the fifth anniversary of its annual independent music festival with Cattyrompus, a special Halloween edition of Sleepy Fest taking place Saturday, October 31, in downtown Durham at The Pinhook and Rubies. 
The festival brings together musicians, DJs, drag performers, visual artists, dancers, puppeteers, and other collaborators for an afternoon-to-late-night celebration of the creative community that has grown around the Carrboro-based independent label. 
The festivities begin at 2 p.m. with The Prowl, featuring live music across both venues through 9 p.m. The evening continues at The Pinhook with the Hell Cat Dance Party, running from 9 p.m. to 2 a.m. 
The lineup includes Twain, Chessa Rich, Lou Hazel, MEGABITCH, Woke County Speedway, DUNUMS, T. Gold, Delver, XOXOK, Amelia Riggs, and Shane Leonard, alongside DJs Fruitti Pebbles, Tuttle Recall, Lomain, and Vera. 
But Cattyrompus is more than a music festival. Throughout the day, attendees can expect a live-scored puppet show, an all-ages costume contest, a Hell Cat-themed mask-making station, visual installations, and other collaborations. At night, Durham drag performers Naomi Dix and Stormie Daie will host the Hell Cat Dance Party, with Strut the Yard bringing a Silent Disco Soul Train to the streets and around downtown. 
Additional special programming includes Club Era with Stormie Daie and Naomi Dix, Stella Rosalie Rosen, Brooks Emanuel, and Heron Toe.

title: Death & Dying Seasonal Tour
location: President James K. Polk Historic Site
description:

You will walk through the steps of a wake with a trained docent who will explain to you the community's response to death, body preparation, the wake, burial and stone cutting techniques. The tour includes a stop in the kitchen house and ends in the cemetery where you will learn the unique history behind the Polk family cemetery.

This tour is designed to be family friendly and suitable for all ages. All tour fees are paid on site prior to the start of the tour.

Tour guests can expect up to a 1/4 mile of walking along some uneven ground. Please wear appropriate shoes and clothing for the weather. In the event of extreme heat, cold or rain, the tour will be cancelled.

A winner of the Naumburg International Piano Competition and recipient of an Avery Fisher Career Grant, he has performed in solo recitals at Carnegie Hall and the Kennedy Center and appeared with leading orchestras across the country.

Through live coaching and musical exploration, Pratt will offer students and audience members a rare look into the interpretive choices, technique, and creative process behind a compelling performance.

This event is free and open to the public. All are welcome.

title: Carolina North Forest Gravel + Gab
description:
Triangle Off Road Cyclists (TORC)
* **Title:** Carolina North Forest Gravel + Gab
* **Intended audience:** The gravel curious to the gravel enthusiast. This is a beginnermediate-level (\*see distance & pace below), no-drop (no one is left behind) ride from Back Alley Bikes over to the gravel roads of Carolina North Forest. Riders with gravel experience are welcome, but **we will prioritize good vibes and comfortable group riding** over speed and intensity.
* **Distance:** 15 miles ([route](https://ridewithgps.com/routes/54012358))
* **Pace:** 10-12 mph and conversational
* **Duration:** About 2.5 hours
* **Meet** @8:45am @ [Back Alley Bikes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Vg8FUof42TmzNb6F6), **Wheels rolling** @ 9am
* Helmets are required
* ***Hot days are dangerous! Please come hydrated, bring plenty of water, and tell a leader if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, clammy, fatigued, cramps, or nausea.***
* **Please fill out the [2026 TORC ride waiver](https://www.torc-nc.org/waiver/).** You only need fill it out 1 time per year.
* Other attire: Attire is good, yes, and whatever floats your boat. Some of us ride in boots, some clip in. Dress for the weather/conditions.
* Water bottle/pack, mini-tool, spare tube/tubeless supplies, and pump/CO2 highly recommended.
* No headphones or other distractions
* Optional coffee and pastries after the ride at [Even Dough Bakery](https://www.evendough.net/_files/ugd/25157a_c98496ddedb04409a2c90324cfab6a22.pdf) (subject to change day-of)
* Message me with any questions you may have.

**HOW TO HELP TORC HELP YOU:**
If you aren't a member of TORC please consider joining. Trails are not cheap to build or easy to maintain. So much goes on behind the scenes at all the trails. If you love trails please [consider joining TORC](https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/) to help support the work TORC does. Not ready to join? You can [donate to TORC](https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/) to support our mission at the bottom of that page.

title: Big Woods Hike
location: Big Woods Private Preserve, Chapel Hill, NC, United States
description:
Join TLC to explore a special Chatham County preserve!
This will be the first public hike at Big Woods Nature Preserve, the second-largest single purchase by TLC in Chatham county. This preserve, which is not open to the public, is also TLC's first acquisition of land directly bordering Jordan Lake's protected land in a decade. 

Nick Adams, TLC's Senior Land Manager West, and TLC Trail Guide, Steve Gartrell, will talk about the ecology of Big Woods and TLC's journey to acquiring the property. Due to the lack of developed trails, this hike requires traversing on uneven ground, steep inclines, and over a small stream crossing. Big Woods has a fairly open understory and rugged topography that hosts mature oak-hickory forests, mixed mesic forests, and a rich floodplain along Bush Creek. This hike will be approximately 2 miles, with about 260 feet of elevation gain. This is a free event, but preregistration is required. Since this is a private property, the exact location will be sent via email after registration.

title: Get Unstuck: Why Change Seemed Hard When It's Really Easy
description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group
Congratulations! You’re on the path of self-improvement with a long list of changes you hope to make to get the life you always wanted. But that idealistic to-do list can inspire and excite you, or make you anxious and depressed. Is it too much to ask for everything from inner peace to world peace, with lots of love, health, wealth and fun times in between? Why is change so hard, especially in a society where so many people seem content to settle for daily violence, ignorance, and self-serving survivalism? Well, you’re not alone in the struggle to stay optimistic in these challenging times. You just need some key insights on how to get unstuck when you’re actually on the threshold of breakthroughs. Join us Sunday Nov 1, 2026 for a free liberating talk on how to see the fabulous growth you’ve already made, so you can relax and let more changes happen to live happy ever after.

These are the ascension times, and knowing what that means can make all the difference. Now is time to become the creator of your own life as you live it, so that you no longer have to die to go to heaven. The traditional model of achievement was based on divine rewards and punishments. Please God in life and get rewarded in the afterlife. Suffer graciously, sacrifice, don’t complain. To this day, many people still work hard and struggle for later rewards. Even if they don’t believe in a parental God, they still believe in employers, economies, and rules to satisfy to collect their benefits someday. Rebels who steal and dominate may seem powerful, but they’re actually so weak that they believe in rules by which they can never win. People who really know how to succeed in life become kind and generous.

Ascension means you stop waiting for someone else to fix your life someday, and start living your own future now. Be in the world but not of it; think and feel from the vision that you hold. The quality of your journey is the destination that you seek, so if you don’t like how you’re living then you’re the only one who can change your own experience. Change is hard when you don’t understand how the living loving Universe works to always support your personal lifestyle. There’s nothing more powerful than how you choose to be. Don’t focus on what you do, focus on how you do everything that you do. Your state of being leads naturally to what you can and will do next. The changes you desire are already happening at every level of reality itself. Deep down every human being is good and just wants a good life. How you let this happen is what must be learned. The gods help those who help themselves.

So while Earth life is extremely challenging, that challenge doesn’t have to be hard. Many people today are feeling challenged as if they’re being attacked on a battlefield. They react accordingly and out of control, causing harm to others and themselves. Instead, you can feel challenged like learning a whole new way to live in the best total immersion college course. Every day is a new exciting lesson in how to be more confident and happy than the day before. Whichever attitude you hold, you will get more of what you expect. Contrary to popular belief, other people are not affecting you, only you affect yourself. If you let other people exist exactly as they choose in order to inform you by their examples of possible choices and consequences, then you alone can decide most consciously what’s best for you.

For this meetup, review your wish list for your life. Have the courage to go beyond the inner critics that say you failed just to make you feel bad about yourself. We’ll see how belief systems work to help you manifest the life that you deep down know you still deserve. Weak people like to think that everything should be just right for them, so they waste their time and energy on trying to control and change the world instead of changing themselves. That’s ok, we can all learn to forgive and change. False negative beliefs say that change is hard, requiring endless subconscious perfection. That way you’ll always fail, never change, and feed the negative energy with your own hurt stuck emotions. True positive beliefs explain what you’ve already done good enough to build upon, so your consciousness is all you ever need. We’ll study the four levels of changes that you must understand to bust every old pattern, and conclude with a guided meditation to invite more divine support for your dreams. The Source wants you to be happy and fulfilled for the highest good of all.

title: Jenny Elder Fitch Memorial Lecture: Digging Deeper into Ecological Horticulture
location: North Carolina Botanical Garden, 100 Old Mason Farm Road, Chapel Hill, NC, 27517, United States
description:
Speaker: Uli Lorimer, Director of Horticulture, Native Plant Trust 
Free; preregistration required 
Join us for this year’s Jenny Elder Fitch Memorial Lecture as Uli Lorimer with the Native Plant Trust explores the questions and challenges shaping ecological horticulture today. 
Successful gardens are being asked to be both beautiful and to provide ecological function. Welcoming more native plants into designed spaces has been shown to provide great benefit for humans and wildlife alike. Environmentally conscious garden decisions are based on assumptions that native plants better support ecosystems, that genetic diversity is essential, and that native cultivars may not be as functional as species. 
This talk will explore the assumptions and the challenges to those assumptions. What role does the nursery industry play in providing the right kinds of information for gardeners to make informed decisions? Do maintenance practices influence biodiversity, and how do science and research factor into these assumptions?

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: CEE Seminar - LEARNING HEART DISEASE: MODELING HEART AND HEART VALVE DISEASE USING NOVEL GPU BASED FINITE ELEMENT APPROACHES
location: None
description: Computational models of cardiac mechanics can serve as vital predictive tools to assist our understanding of cardiac pathologies. For example, we have developed a novel pipeline to convert pre-operative clinical images of the mitral valve into predictive patient specific models capable of accurately predicting the post-repair state. However, the slow computational speed of traditional finite element models limits their practical clinical application. We have previously demonstrated the efficacy of the neural network finite element (NNFE) approach for predicting cardiac mechanics of an idealized left ventricle within clinically relevant timeframes without compromising accuracy. In this work, we demonstrate that the NNFE approach can 1) predict the complex deformation patterns arising due to the presence of infarct tissue, 2) predict the effects of infarct occurring in varying locations and of varying sizes, and 3) capture the compensatory mechanisms of the healthy tissue that displays a higher contractile level in order to maintain stroke volume. These results represent an important first step towards high-speed patient specific infarct modeling. While still in its early stages, this approach paves the pathway for high-speed patient-specific clinical simulations.

title: Chemistry Defense: Hung-Min Lin:"Dynamical Correlations and Transport in Superionic Argyrodites"
location: None
description:
Superionic conductors are crystalline solids exhibiting liquid-like ionic diffusivity, making them promising for solid-state battery applications. Yet, the atomistic mechanisms governing their transport properties remain poorly understood.  Here, I combine neutron scattering experiments with atomistic simulations to investigate the atomic structure and dynamics underlying ionic diffusion in argyrodite-type superionic materials.

I first investigate collective ionic hopping, long proposed as an origin of superionicity. Neutron scattering measurements on single-crystal Cu7PS6 reveal short-range dynamical correlations among diffusing ions, providing direct experimental evidence of collective hopping and resolving its spatiotemporal characteristics. Machine-learned molecular dynamics simulations reproduce these observations and provide complementary insights into the hopping mechanism. By tracking the dynamical structure factor across the superionic transition, we further establish that collective hopping emerges from the breakdown of low-energy, Cu-dominated phonons in the ordered phase. These results establish a direct connection between precursor phonons and collective hopping, with similar behavior observed across several Ag- and Cu-based argyrodites. Our analysis also reveals that spectral weight transfer from phonons to collective hopping gives rise to liquid-like dynamics, marked by a crossover in the low-energy vibrational density of states from quadratic to linear scaling. Together, these findings pinpoint strongly anharmonic phonons as a common origin of collective hopping and liquid-like dynamics.

Next, I investigate the role of the host lattice in enabling fast ionic diffusion in Li argyrodites, technologically important solid electrolytes. We show that framework disorder and dynamics play distinct but cooperative roles. Static disorder creates percolating pathways for Li-ion diffusion, while host-lattice fluctuations dynamically open local bottlenecks. This cooperative mechanism provides a microscopic design principle for high-performance solid electrolytes.

Taken together, these studies establish the microscopic origins of ionic transport in superionic argyrodites and highlight the role of dynamical correlations. These findings go beyond conventional descriptions based on static potential energy surfaces for ionic hopping and provide microscopic insights into superionic transport.

title: Critical Classicality: Book Talk and Poetry Reading
location: Rubenstein Library Holsti-Anderson Family Assembly Room 153
description:
In this talk, Kelly Nguyen shares the story behind her book, Critical Classicality in Vietnam and the Diaspora (Oxford University Press, 2026), and the poetry that emerged alongside it. The book traces how Vietnamese writers and thinkers have engaged with Greco-Roman antiquity, developing the concept of critical classicality: a way of confronting the classical tradition's complicity in colonialism and empire while also asking how those historically marginalized by that tradition might reclaim and remake it for their own liberatory purposes.
But what happens when the histories we study refuse to stay on the page? Nguyen turns from scholarship to poetry, sharing select poems that were written alongside the book as a way of metabolizing the violence, silences, and trauma of the archives. Reimagining the Homeric Odyssey through the experiences of Vietnamese refugees, including her own and those of her parents, these poems put critical classicality into practice. The event concludes with a conversation with graduate students in Comparative Literature and Classics.

Reception to follow in Allen 103A.

REGISTER TO ATTEND!

Stitching Strength is a documentary film that captures the fight against ALS - a terminal disease that strips away the body's control - through lens of creativity, courage, and connection.

At its heart is Dr. Richard Bedlack, a neurologist whose bold fashion and bolder optimism set the tone for a radically different kind of care. But this isn't just his story. It's about the patients who refuse to be defined by their diagnosis, and the families who turn grief into art, music, and action.

This is not a story of surrender. It's a story of style, strength, and the power of believing in what's still possible. For Dr. Bedlack, fashion isn't just how you dress - it's an expression of joy. A conversation starter. A shield against despair. It's medicine. Clothing becomes a way for patients to reclaim their identity, adorn themselves with dignity, and express the parts of themselves ALS can't touch. Style becomes a tool for healing, not just expression. From accessible runway designs to custom suits lined with symbolism, every stitch is an act of strength. Read more about Stitching Strength.

Opening reception will feature DJ GrayGray from House Music for ALS.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: The Bettie Allison Rand Lectures in Art History: Alexander Marr, University of Cambridge
location: Hyde Hall, University Room
description:
Pictorial Intelligence in Renaissance Art: Holbein’s Wit

 

The Renaissance witnessed intense debate about the nature and location of human intelligence. When it came to artists, this was focused on natural endowments versus trained skill, the relationship between the mind and the hand, and—especially among humanists—whether pictorial art was capable of intelligent authorship as opposed to mere replication of the visible world. Taking Hans Holbein the Younger as a case study, this lecture will explore how the mindful hand of a supremely gifted painter could demonstrate the inherent ingenuity and playful wit of an inventive--rather than merely mimetic--artistic intelligence. 

 

Alexander Marr is University Professor of Renaissance and Early Modern Art. He specializes in European art 1400-1800, especially its intellectual and literary aspects in their social contexts. His most recent publication is Holbein's Wit: Pictorial Ingenuity in Renaissance Art.

 

Before coming to Cambridge, he taught at the University of Southern California and the University of St Andrews. From 2014 to 2019, he was Director of the project Genius before Romanticism: Ingenuity in Early Modern Art & Science, funded by an ERC Consolidator Grant. His awards include a Paul Mellon Centre Senior Fellowship, the Robert H. Smith Residency at the V&A, and a Philip Leverhulme Prize. He was the founding Director of Cambridge Visual Culture (CVC). In 2024, he delivered the Pharos Lectures at the University of Oxford.

 

Through a generous gift to the UNC Arts and Sciences Foundation, William G. Rand established this lecture series in memory of his late wife, Bettie Allison Rand. This funding enables the Department of Art and Art History to invite one or more eminent art historians to UNC-CH every other year for residencies of various lengths. While they are in Chapel Hill, these scholars present a series of lectures and interact with undergraduate and graduate art history and studio art students.

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Contact: Christoph Brachmann, cbrachma@email.unc.edu   

 

This event is eligible for CLE credit.

title: Trail Tuesday night ride....casual style ... at Williamson Preserve
description:
Triangle Off Road Cyclists (TORC)
***PLEASE CHECK https://www.trianglemtb.com/ FOR TRAIL STATUS.***\*

If the trail is closed the ride is canceled.
\*\*\*\*BRING LIGHTS!!!!!!!!!!\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

This is NOT a true beginner mountain biker friendly ride.

This is a good ride for those new to night riding or those who just want to check it out.

This is a **casual** no drop ride for riders who want to ride and socialize. This is not a race or a Strava KOM fest.

We normally split into 2 groups if there are enough riders.... a casual group and a super casual group.
Both groups will be no drop and will stop to regroup often to ensure no one is left behind.

We will meet between 5:30-5:45pm and hit the trail at 6:00pm.
We hang out to chitchat after the ride ... (sometimes with hot cocoa and baked goods) so come for the ride, stay for the laughs (and cocoa).

**Traffic sucks on the way to Williamson so give yourself more time to get there then you think you will need. Please be ready to ride at 6:00pm**

We will meet at the white barn on the opposite side of the church from the main trail head parking lot. Parking here is by special permission for the ride. (Parking here without special permission from TLC is not allowed and considered trespassing so please only park here with TLC's permission.)

PLEASE SEE THE LINK BELOW FOR PARKING. DO NOT PARK AT THE REGULAR PARKING LOT.

https://www.google.com/maps/place/35%C2%B043'57.9%22N+78%C2%B026'54.0%22W/@35.7327613,-78.4505187,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x0:0x0!7e2!8m2!3d35.7327571!4d-78.4483296

Mountain bike, helmet, and light are required.
NO ONE CAN RIDE WITHOUT A HELMET.
Gloves, water bottle/pack, mini-tool, spare tube, and pump/CO2 highly recommended.

Message me with any questions you may have.

Please fill out the 2026 TORC ride waiver. The link is below. It only needs to be filled out 1 time per year.

https://www.webscorer.com/register?raceid=415052

**HOW TO HELP TORC HELP YOU:**
If you aren't a member of TORC please consider joining. Trails are not cheap to build or easy to maintain. So much goes on behind the scenes at all the trails. If you love trails please consider joining TORC to help support the work TORC does. You may join TORC at https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/

Also please consider donating to Triangle Land Conservancy (TLC). https://www.triangleland.org/give/donate

P.S. All the cool kids wear mismatched socks on Trail Tuesday.

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the People's Solidarity Hub at 1809 Chapel Hill Rd, Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

Readers are:
• Rachel
• Ruth
• Tricia

Backup Readers are:
• Rob

Deep Backup:
• Heather

***

***We meet every Tuesday at the same time, but alternate between In-Person*** ***and on Zoom. Members may attend both formats, if desired, but readers will be listed separately under the In-Person or Zoom weeks.***

title: Astronomy On Tap - Science Talk & Trivia
location: Fullsteam ATC, 320 Blackwell St #101, Durham, 27701
description:
Come check out Astronomy on Tap Triangle (AoTT), our North Carolina chapter of serving up short, engaging talks about astronomy over beer! For this 10th season of AoTT, we’ll be in Fullsteam-ATC’s beautiful new location at the Boiler Room at the historic American Tobacco Campus (ATC) in downtown Durham. Events will be held on the first Tuesday of the month and are free and open to the public. 
Our third event of the semester will be held on Tuesday, November 3rd, from 7:00-8:45 PM! Talks details are included below. Grab a drink (or two) at Fullsteam-ATC and head to their 100-seat theater for a night filled with astronomy, trivia, and fun. Free parking (after 5 PM) is available in the North and South Parking Decks surrounding the American Tobacco Campus. If an attendant asks for payment during a special event (e.g., baseball game), just let them know you’re there to visit Fullsteam Brewery, and they should wave you through. 
“Tuning into the Cosmic Symphony with Pulsar Timing Arrays”
Dr. Caitlin Witt (Wake Forest University)
In the cosmic symphony of gravitational waves, supermassive black hole binaries provide the bass notes. However, when these colossal duos play all at once, their individual melodies overlap into an indistinct rumble. Astronomers have at last found evidence for this background hum of gravitational waves using an observatory that spans our galaxy, but more faint signals lurk out there in the universe waiting to be uncovered. Tune in to hear more about gravitational wave symphonies, monstrous black holes, colliding galaxies, dead stars, and more!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: What Enterprise AI Looks Like When It Works
description:
All Things AI (Live)
In this session of *Newsweek’s* “AI Impact Forum,” **Dr. Ranjit Tinaikar** sits down with **Firdaus Bhathena**, executive vice president and chief technology and transformation officer at S&P Global, to examine what it takes to turn advances in AI into meaningful business impact.
Drawing on Bhathena's experience leading technology and transformation at S&P Global and previously at FIS Global and CVS Health, the conversation will explore why trusted, differentiated data becomes increasingly important as powerful AI models become more widely available—and what companies need to do to put that data to work.
Bhathena and Tinaikar will discuss moving beyond experimentation, making data governed and reusable, redesigning workflows around new capabilities and balancing speed with trust, security and resilience. They will also examine how leaders can keep technology initiatives focused on customer problems and identify where genuine competitive advantage can emerge.

Designed for CEOs, CIOs, CTOs, transformation leaders and senior technology decision-makers, the session will offer a practical look at the choices organizations face as they move AI deeper into their operations and pursue measurable business impact.

title: History for Lunch: The Role of Baptisteries in Byzantine Pilgrimage Sites of the Levant

description: Dr. Robert W. Smith, the Distinguished Professor of History at Mid-Atlantic Christian University, will take participants from modern baptismal practices of congregations in eastern North Carolina to Byzantine baptisteries in the Holy Land. While modern Christians in the United States may undergo multiple baptisms, "rebaptism" was a capital offense under the Law Code of the Byzantine Empire. This presentation will propose an explanation for how the baptisteries of pilgrimage facilities functioned legally in the Levant. Dr. Smith has conducted archaeological excavations at the ancient city of Abila, Jordan, since 1984, including the city’s pilgrimage complex.

description:

Chronic worry that begins to impact the quality of life becomes “anxiety,” and well-intended suggestions to “stop worrying” or applying common stress management techniques are mostly ineffective.

title: Context Over Compute: The Overlooked Lever for AI ROI
description:
Data Science Raleigh
Most enterprises chasing AI ROI look first at bigger models and more compute—but the biggest gains often come from a more economical, less glamorous lever: better context. Pilots stall and production systems underperform not because the models aren't capable, but because they aren't given the right information at the right time, forcing costly rework, manual review, and lost trust.

This webinar reframes context engineering as a business decision rather than a purely technical one. We'll unpack where context investment delivers outsized returns compared to model upgrades, how to identify where context gaps are silently draining value from existing AI initiatives, and how leading teams are prioritizing context work to accelerate time-to-value.

**Key Takeaways:**

1️⃣ **The Real ROI Driver:** Why context—not raw model power—is often the fastest path to measurable AI returns.

2️⃣ **Diagnosing Hidden Costs:** How to spot context gaps that quietly inflate rework, review, and support costs.

3️⃣ **Prioritization Frameworks:** How to decide where to invest in context versus other AI improvements.

4️⃣ **Scaling Value:** Strategies for sustaining ROI gains as AI initiatives expand across the business.

**[Register here](https://datasciconnect.com/events/webinars/context-over-compute/)**

title: FOA Annual Meeting: Remembering the American Revolution in the Cherokee Homeland
description:
FOA Annual Meeting & Program presentation this year is Remembering the American Revolution in the Cherokee Homeland.

Commemorating the American Revolution poses particular challenges if one lives in far Western North Carolina. Here in the Cherokee ancestral homelands, the Revolution brought a bitter and destructive conflict over Cherokee land, with a portion of the Cherokee population entering the war as members of a British-allied coalition of Indigenous peoples. That war, in turn, belonged to a much longer struggle to protect Cherokee land and the wellbeing of Cherokee communities – a struggle that preceded the Revolution and continued long after 1776. In this presentation, Shana Bushyhead Condill (Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians), Executive Director of the Museum of the Cherokee People, and Andrew Denson, professor of history at Western Carolina University, will discuss the challenges involved in remembering the Revolution in the mountain region. In particular, they will examine the planning and creation of the Museum of the Cherokee People’s current exhibition, Unrelenting: Cherokee People and the American Revolution. Register for the program before November 04.

A brief presentation of Friends of the Archives business will follow the program at approximately 3 p.m.

title: Porcelains and Power: The Politics of Chinese Art in the Age of American Ascendancy
location: Ackland Art Museum, 101 S. Columbia Street, Chapel Hill, NC, 27514, United States
description:
A talk by Dr. Ian Shin (Department of American Culture, University of Michigan), co-sponsored with the Department of History. 
How can we understand the relationship between art collecting and Western imperialism as more than simply a story of victim and aggressor, of the plundered and the plunderer? From the Gilded Age to World War II, elite collectors and museums in the United States transformed from owning a smattering of Chinese porcelains to possessing some of the world’s largest and most sophisticated collections of Chinese art. 
In this talk, historian Ian Shin shows that, beyond aesthetic taste and economics, geopolitics were vital to this transformation. Collecting and studying Chinese art honed Americans’ belief that they should dominate Asia and the Pacific Ocean through the ideology of “imperial stewardship.” U.S. imperial stewardship encompassed both genuine curiosity and care for Chinese art, and the enduring structures of domination that underpinned the growing transpacific art market in the early twentieth century. Far more than a history of cultural “exchange” between the United States and China, this is also a history of rivalries and feuds with European curators and enterprising Chinese merchants. 
Ultimately, this talk challenges us to come to terms with how our interest in and desire for beautiful art are inextricable from questions of power. 
Free, but space is limited; registration required below. 
  
This event is part of UNC–Chapel Hill’s Campus Life Experience (CLE) program. Students who attend can scan the QR code provided at the event to receive CLE credit.

title: Team ENOUGH Welcome Session (For Young People Under 26)
location: Virtual event
description:
Link to join: https://www.mobilize.us/join/46980103/1:289c10553229276350cc658c9aadbfdd411190b12e08cda6a01d43e12a5ee036/

How to join:
Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Nov 5 - Visual AI Agriculture Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics at the intersection of agriculture and AI.

**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 05, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/visual-ai-agriculture-meetup-november-5-2026)**

Talks will include:

**U-Net Framework for Micro-Scale Surface Damage Segmentation in High-Resolution Soybean Seed Imagery**

Accurate detection of surface-level seed damage is critical for soybean seed quality assurance, yet automated micro-scale damage detection in high-resolution imagery remains an open challenge due to extreme spatial variability in damage scale, severe class imbalance across damage types, and the computational demands of processing ultra-high resolution agricultural imagery at scale. This research addresses the semantic segmentation of fine-grained soybean seed surface defects, such as wrinkles, dark spots, and general surface damage, in 6048 × 4024 pixel images where target damages can be as small as 18 × 18 pixels, using an augmented dataset of 77,000 individual seed images.

To overcome the difficulties of micro-scale detection, spatial sparsity, and class confusion, we propose a two-stage training and dual model inference framework built on an optimized U-Net architecture with a ResNet34 encoder. In the first stage, a damage specialist model is trained using weighted loss functions and a class-balanced approach that prioritizes damage classes.

In the second stage, transfer learning is applied to initialize a healthy seed specialist model from Stage 1 weights, with rebalanced class weights and tile probabilities that identify healthy seeds. During inference, a confidence-gated damage filter suppresses low-confidence predictions, and healthy seed labels are assigned only when the specialist model's confidence exceeds that of the damage model.

The two specialist models achieve validation accuracies of 94% and 98.53%, respectively, and the combined inference system successfully detects and localizes all three damage categories across unseen test images under conditions of extreme spatial variability and class imbalance. Qualitative evaluation confirms close alignment of predicted boundaries with ground truth annotations across all damage types, including dark spots.

These results demonstrate that confidence-gated dual model inference can reduce class confusion in imbalanced micro-scale segmentation, advancing the feasibility of fine-grained automated seed quality inspection at the scale.

*About the Speaker*

[Saurav Upadhyaya](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sauravupadhyaya/) is an AI/ML researcher with a Master's degree in Computer Science, whose work spans agricultural AI, conversational systems, and public health, consistently translating advanced technology into tangible real-world impact.

**From camera to drone: wildfire detection and integration at the edge**

Wildfires are getting larger and more expensive every year. But caught early, a fire is a small job for a small team; caught late, nothing stops it. The cameras to catch them are already installed, so the work is not necessary more sensors but making the ones we have act.

This talk walks the whole chain: a small vision model running on the camera that flags smoke, an integration layer that scores the alert against terrain, weather and history to decide whether it matters, and a drone dispatched to confirm before anyone commits a crew. We will cover what has to run at the edge and why, how small the model can get before it stops seeing smoke, and what it takes to trust a detection nobody has looked at yet.

*About the Speaker*

[Maxime Carriere](https://voxel51.com/events/www.linkedin.com/in/maxime-carriere-871756161) is co-founder of Kernwerk in Berlin, where he works on compressing AI models to run on cheap embedded hardware.

**5,000 Flights to Answer One Question: Can a Drone Sample as Well as a Human?**

Environmental testing still begins with a person walking onto a site with a shovel. We built a system that turns a plain-language brief into a sampling campaign, flies it, and returns soil, water and vegetation samples with GPS, timestamps and chain of custody intact: 5,000 flights, roughly 9,000 miles and 570 flight hours over a 185-acre site in Roatan, much of it under canopy where GPS degrades and clearances are tight.

I will walk through the vision and planning stack, including multispectral and thermal canopy sensing, terrain and land-cover mapping, and the constraint solver that clears a route against airspace and battery budget before anything leaves the ground. Then the harder problem: evidentiary comparability.

A drone-collected result means nothing to a regulator unless it agrees with a hand-collected split under the same method, so I will show the dual-collection protocol we designed to test exactly that. I will close on why calibrated uncertainty and knowing when a model should refuse to answer matter more than raw accuracy once the output lands in a regulatory filing.

*About the Speaker*

[Rohan Talwadia](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rohantalwadia/) is co-founder and CTO of LabGPT, which automates environmental field sampling using drones and edge analysis, with results returned through ISO/IEC 17025-accredited partner laboratories.

title: Psychological Avoidance & Its Impact on Your Mental Health
description:
Anxiety is a highly uncomfortable feeling, a lingering presence that causes physical and mental tension, fills the mind with endless “what ifs,” and is capable of spiralling into episodes of paralyzing anxiety attacks. People with anxiety will typically focus on reducing or eliminating it as the main problem, whereas the real problem may lie elsewhere, with psychological avoidance. Psychological avoidance is a quick fix to anxiety. It offers immediate emotional relief, but it’s fleeting and comes at a heavy cost. When we avoid certain situations, decisions, or actions, it can ultimately lead to even greater anxiety and additional problems.
