title: Hanes Visiting Artist Lecture Series: Sheida Soleimani
location: Hamilton Hall, 100
description:
Department of Art and Art History

 

Sheida Soleimani is an Iranian-American artist who lives in Providence. The daughter of political refugees who were persecuted by the Iranian government in the early 1980s, Soleimani makes work that melds sculpture, collage and photography and highlights her own critical perspective on historical and contemporary socio-political occurrences in Iran. She focuses on media trends and the dissemination of societal occurrences in the news, adapting images from popular press and social media leaks to exist within alternate scenarios. Her work has been recognized internationally in both exhibitions and publications such as Artforum, The New York Times, The Huffington Post, Interview, and VICE Magazine.

 

Soleimani is an Associate Professor of Fine Arts at Brandeis University and a 2026 Guggenheim Fellow.

 

An endowment established in 1983 through the generosity of Nancy and Robin Hanes supports the Art Department's Visiting Artist Series. This important program brings both established and emerging artists to campus to discuss their work in public lectures and to offer individual critiques to our M.F.A. students.  The Hanes Visiting Artist series greatly enriches both our academic programs and our outreach to the wider community.  All lectures are free and open to the public.

title: The Ritual of Belonging: 35 Years of the Friday Center
location: William and Ida Friday Center
description:
Come. Connect. Celebrate.

 

In 1991, UNC President William C. Friday opened the doors to what he called "the citizens' classroom," a place built to make learning and connection open to everyone, with or without a UNC degree. Named for Bill and Ida Friday, two North Carolinians defined by their service to education and public life, the Friday Center was founded on a simple belief: learning never stops.

For 35 years, the Friday Center has carried that belief forward by opening doors, bringing people together, and extending Carolina's knowledge beyond the traditional classroom. It is a place where the University and the community meet, where ideas are shared, relationships are built, and learning becomes part of a larger public life.

This November, we're celebrating 35 years with an evening centered on something that has always been essential to the Friday Center: the power of gathering, and the belonging it creates.

Joining us is Casper ter Kuile, author of The Power of Ritual and co-founder of Sacred Design Lab.

 

THE POWER OF RITUAL

Amidst rising rates of disconnection, what are the rituals that gather us together? How can we deepen our relationships, make meaningful connections, and experience joyful belonging? Join author and co-founder of Sacred Design Lab Casper ter Kuile for an evening's conversation on the power of ritual. You'll explore how to cultivate the containers of connection at home, on campus, and in the wider community. Learn how ritual can weave us back into a fabric of common life.

 

The Evening

6:30pm | Director's reception, join us for refreshments and conversation
7:15pm | Casper's talk, followed by a live Q&A

 

This is a free event, but space is limited, and registration is required to attend.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

title: Getting Proper about Prompting:  An Introduction to Prompt Engineering for Social Science and Survey Research
description:
Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content.  Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries.  Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’”  Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting.  Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process.  In this short course we will provide an overview of the emerging field of prompt engineering and illustrate how a prompt engineering approach and problem specification mindset can be useful for maximizing the utility of large language models, specifically, within social science.  Concepts and experimental approaches will be illustrated using several real-world, grounded and published work.  The shortcourse also incorporates an experiential component that encourages participants to apply basic concepts that we cover in the course in real-time as we work on exercises together in the later part of the course.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Teen Science Café: Rhino Conservation
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
One of the many tools used in conservation is translocation – moving individual animals or plants to a new area. They can be moved to establish new populations, increase existing numbers, or to remove an ongoing threat. While it can bring many benefits, translocation requires careful planning to ensure individuals thrive in their new habitat. This is especially true with endangered black rhinos, so conservation partners carefully study how animals behave, their genetic health, and source populations prior to conducting translocations. Listen to our own Dr. Liz Kierepka, as she talks about her work with the species. 
Teen Science Cafés bring teens together in an informal setting to learn about science and technology, on the first Friday every month during the school year. Each event includes a presentation, related activity, Q&A session and time to socialize with other participants. This is a free program recommended for ages 11–17. Cafés will be held in person at the Daily Planet Cafe and streamed live on YouTube. 
About the presenter: 

–
Dr. Liz Kierepka is the Head of our Genomics and Microbiology Research Lab and Associate Research Professor at North Carolina State University. Dr. Kierepka is involved with multiple projects within mammals including evaluating genomics of island Peromyscus mice, rabies and urban adaptation in raccoons, population estimation of coyotes on the Outer Banks, and pedigree reconstruction in black rhinos.

description:
FEATURING

Nicholas DiEguenio, violin
Mimi Solomon, piano

 

PROGRAM

Featuring Allen Anderson’s “Linen,” plus Beethoven Violin Sonatas Nos. 6 and 7

This season, Gut Instinct takes on the large-scale project “To Beethoven Rather Than To Seem,” marking 200 years since Beethoven’s death and 250 since the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Over the course of five concerts, Nicholas DiEugenio and pianist Mimi Solomon will present all ten Beethoven Sonatas on period instruments along with five commissioned works written expressly for them.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

 

The Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project, now in its third season, is a concert series in the Triangle area which brings UNC-Chapel Hill and Duke University’s historical instrument collections together with artists committed to presenting inspired, visceral, historically informed performances of the 19th-century chamber music repertoire. The series features music of female composers and their artistic circles. The name “Gut Instinct” is a play on words. In 19th-century Europe, the violin, viola, and cello were strung with (sheep) gut.

 

All of the artists collaborating with the Pleyel and Graf pianos at UNC-Chapel Hill (built in 19th-century Paris and Vienna, respectively), as well as the Clementi piano at Duke (early 19th-century England) use these gut string materials. The turn of phrase “gut instinct” also refers to the visceral, accessible nature of the musical performances that this series presents. Our mission is to make “Historically Informed Performance” accessible, relatable, and culturally relevant! We also want to feature these special pianos that are rarely heard by the public, along with great music by female composers which has remained lesser known to the greater public for far too long, and living composers who are keeping our art form alive!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

title: Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Day
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
The NC Museum of Natural Sciences is a research-based museum with Museum staff who conduct novel research and steward our collections. Our Research Highlight Days feature these researchers and their fields of study. 
This event will be held on the first and third floors of the Nature Research Center. 
Join us as we celebrate Astronomy and Astrophysics Research at this event! 

Presentations
11 AM Observing Massive Stars in the Galaxy
Dr. Rachel Smith, NC Museum of Natural Sciences 
Dr. Rachel Smith will present her current research on the formation of planetary systems in the Galaxy. Highlights will be recent observations of massive young stars, including a unique “runaway” star, obtained with the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility in Hawaii. 
Rachel Smith is an observational astronomer who is interested in how planetary systems form and evolve. She focuses on the chemical pathways that lead to Earth-like planets and the molecules needed for life. Rachel uses large ground-based observatories to gather spectra from stars in giant molecular clouds — nearby factories for new stars and planets. Rachel is especially interested in how data from young stars connect to the formation of our own solar system about 4.6 billion years ago.
Rachel is Head the Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Lab and Curator of Meteorites at the NC Museum of Natural Sciences. She is also a Professor in the Dept. of Physics & Astronomy at Appalachian State University, and is an Adjunct Professor at UNC-Chapel Hill. 
12 PM Making Sense of Spiral Galaxies: How Volunteers and AI Team Up to Identify Individual Spiral Arms
Dr. Patrick Treuthardt, NC Museum of Natural Sciences 
The winding arms of spiral galaxies are one of their most obvious features. By measuring how tightly the arms are wrapped, we can reveal clues about other components that are much harder to observe, such as dark matter content and central black hole mass. By partnering volunteers with AI, we aim to identify individual spiral arms in tens of thousands of galaxies, measure how tightly each arm is wound, and use those measurements to estimate these elusive properties. Doing so will help us better understand how galaxies similar to our own Milky Way form and evolve. 
Dr. Patrick Treuthardt is the Assistant Head of the Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Lab at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and a Research Affiliate in the Department of Computing Sciences at Coastal Carolina University. He studies the shapes and structures of nearby galaxies as well as the underlying physics that produces them. He is also the lead researcher of the Spiral Graph citizen science project and its follow-up, Cluster Buster. 

Exhibits and Activities
Spiral Graph: Cluster Buster
We will demonstrate and discuss Spiral Graph: Cluster Buster, our online citizen science project dedicated to identifying individual arms in spiral galaxies and measuring their winding. The degree of winding serves as a proxy for properties such as the mass of the dark matter halo and the mass of the black hole found in a galaxy’s nucleus. Our goal is to find galaxies that will help us understand the co-formation and co-evolution of spiral galaxies and their central supermassive black holes. 
Raleigh Astronomy Club
RAC will have a table with astronomy related handouts and will answer questions about astronomy and telescopes. 
Discovering New Worlds: The Science of Exploring Space
NASA/JPL Solar System Ambassadors
From distant exoplanets far beyond our solar system to galaxies at the edge of the observable universe, scientists are constantly uncovering new worlds and new mysteries. Meet a NASA/JPL Solar System Ambassador and learn how astronomers use observations, technology, and scientific research to explore our universe. 
Astrophysics Research Highlights
This table will showcase new student research by undergraduates in Physics & Astronomy at Appalachian State University.
3rd Floor 
Visitors from Space: Meteorites from Asteroids, the Moon, and Mars
We will showcase several meteorites from the Museum collection, including new samples from the asteroid belt, the Moon, and Mars.

title: Opening Celebration of Grounded by Maya Freelon
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description:
Join us for a fun-filled afternoon at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design to celebrate the opening of Grounded by acclaimed artist Maya Freelon. 

Drawing on her signature use of delicate tissue paper, Freelon transforms the galleries into an immersive environment that honors both fragility and resilience. In Grounded, the red clay and soil of North Carolina become central materials and metaphors, asking us to consider what it means to create sanctuary in uncertain times and how the land itself holds memory, pain, and possibility.

The community celebration will include local organizations highlighting African American heritage and wellness, along with special performances by Tre. Charles, Johnny Lee Chapman III, and NC State’s Panoramic Dance Project. 

You are invited to Connect. Celebrate. Get Grounded. Please read more about the timed activities below.

Celebration Program Schedule

1 p.m. | Celebration Begins
Ongoing Activities 1–5 p.m.

Discover everything happening across the lawn, garden, and museum! Create your own contribution to our Community Tissue Paper Quilt in the Grounded exhibition, meet local partners, and enjoy food from the Empanadas and More Food Truck. Complimentary non-alcoholic drinks are available while supplies last, plus FREE Howling Cow ice cream for our first 200 visitors!

1:15–1:45 p.m. | Panoramic Dance Performance
Adams Gallery
Enjoy a performance inspired by Grounded choreographed by Christa Oliver and performed by NC State students in the Department of Performing Arts & Technology and featuring Atiba Rorie and Khalid Saleem. Standing room viewing only; seating available upon accommodation request.

1:50-2:10 p.m. | Opening Remarks
Main Lobby
Hear remarks from artist-in-residence Maya Freelon, Museum Director Sara Segerlin and special guests. Standing room viewing only; seating available upon accommodation request.

2:15–3:45 p.m. | Tre. Charles & Band
Museum Lawn
Bring a lawn chair or a blanket and sit on the lawn to enjoy live music by Durham-based artist Tre. Charles and his guest band. 

2:45–3 p.m. and 3:30–3:45 p.m. | Spoken Word with Johnny Lee Chapman III
Black-Sanderson Gallery
Meet Raleigh Poet Laureate Johnny Lee Chapman III in the Crafting Sanctuaries exhibition. Limited seating; extra seating available upon accommodation request. 

3:45–4:15 p.m. | Panoramic Dance Performance
Adams Galleryand Woodson Galleries
Enjoy a second performance by Christa Oliver and NC State students (details above)..

4–5 p.m. | Ask Me! Guide
Historic Chancellor’s Residence
Meet Khadija McNair, manager of NC Freedom Park, near the fireplace and ask about Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina Black Heritage.

5 p.m. | Celebration Concludes

description:
This event is free to attend, but registration is requested. 

Join local astronomers with the Greensboro Astronomy Club as we observe the night skies over the Iron Ore Belt Access. Attendees may expect to see closer-than-typical views of the moon, planets, star clusters, and other celestial objects subject to change with time of year and local sky darkness.

Telescopes and viewing equipment will be set up on site but you may wish to bring your own binoculars or telescope, plus a chair or blanket for seating. Dress for the weather. Flashlights & headlamps should have a red-light option or filter to protect your night vision.

Skywatching sessions may be cancelled at the last minute for weather. Please register at the Register link so you can be emailed in the event of cancellation.

Program equipment and instruction provided by members of the Greensboro Astronomy Club, which meet the third Friday of each month at the Greensboro Science Center. Learn more about their organization here: 

https://greensboroastronomyclub.org/

Star-gazing Etiquette:

Please use a red light at the observing session and keep any light pointed at the ground. As your eyes adapt, a light is not needed at all.Pease do not touch any telescopes or other equipment unless permission is given and form a orderly line behind each telescope. Please do not allow children or pets to run around the observing area. Pets must be on a leash no longer than 6 feet at all times. This is to protect others' safety and the equipment.Stock photo © Pexels / Lucas Pezeta

title: Toshi Reagon EcoTones
location: Memorial Hall
description:
Some performances entertain. Others leave audiences seeing the world differently. In EcoTones, music, storytelling, research, personal history, and lived experience come together in an experience that feels less like a performance and more like a gathering. Warm, joyful, and challenging, the work invites audiences to consider what happens when different worlds meet and what becomes possible in the spaces between them.

 

Inspired by the ecological concept of an ecotone—the place where distinct ecosystems overlap and create the conditions for new life—EcoTones explores the intersections that shape our lives, communities, and futures. The result is a shared act of discovery that reveals unexpected connections and invites audiences to see familiar questions from new perspectives.

 

Created by Toshi Reagon in collaboration with UNC-Chapel Hill scholars Danielle Spurlock and Danielle Purifoy and Durham-based writer, scholar, and activist Alexis Pauline Gumbs, the performance places artists and researchers side by side on stage. Their stories, questions, ideas, and experiences become part of the work itself, reflecting Toshi’s belief that important voices and perspectives in our communities belong in shared public conversation.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/toshireagon-ecotones/

In this session, learn how to grow the spectacular chrysanthemums on display at the Festival of Fabulous Mums. See samples of chrysanthemums at various growth stages as you learn the basic horticultural elements involved in growing them. Learn about the 13 classes of mums, how to obtain new plants and their requirements for soil, light, water and fertilizer. With this introduction, you will be ready to grow these incredible blooms in your garden. 
As a longtime chrysanthemum grower, a National Chrysanthemum Society judge, and former president of Central Carolina Chrysanthemum Society, Joan Matthews presents engaging educational programs on the cultivation, exhibition and history of chrysanthemums.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

title: Digital Accessibility Pop-Up Labs
location: Carolina Union, 2502
description:
The POP Lab is a drop-in workspace where UNC faculty and staff can make progress with support from digital accessibility consultants. Bring your documents, course materials, websites, reports, or questions, and work at your own pace. Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.

 

Progress Over Perfection

Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. Digital accessibility depends on steady, intentional progress, not perfection, to expand access for all.

title: Nov 9 - Agentic Labeling for Specialized Visual Data
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 09, 2026
9:00 AM - 10:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/when-prompting-beats-training-agentic-labeling-for-specialized-visual-data-november-9-2026)**

Frontier multimodal models handle familiar concepts well and struggle on niche ones: sorting drill-core samples into 35 geological classes, or telling adhesion from scarring on a ceramic substrate. Our study across 11 specialized visual datasets in manufacturing inspection, geology, and medical imaging found that a few labeled examples in the prompt can close much of that gap, and it also found where that stops working.

**What you’ll learn:**

* Niche versus hard: how in-context examples supply domain knowledge a model is missing, and how to tell a niche task from a genuinely hard one
* What the study measured: on an industrial defect task, one labeled example per class raised macro-F1 from 34% to 59% with no fine-tuning, while on other tasks trained specialists pulled ahead at 5 to 10 examples per class
* Building a few-shot labeling task: define classes, pick reference examples, preview predictions on a small batch, and refine the instructions
* Finding the crossover point: when to stop prompting a foundation model and train a specialist on bootstrapped labels
* Running it on your own data: attendees get free GPU compute from Nebius to try the workflow after the session
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: First Amendment Panel
location: Wilson Library , Pleasants Family Assembly Room
description:
Chair of the Faculty Michael Gerhardt is hosting a panel on the First Amendment and how it protects free expression on our campus. All faculty, staff and students are invited to attend.

 

Suzanne Globetti (moderator) is a teaching associate professor in the political science department at UNC. She teaches courses in American government, including the introductory course, campaigns and elections, and analyzing public opinion.

 

Prior to joining the UNC faculty, she taught at Bowdoin College and Vanderbilt University, where she received the Harriet S. Gilliam Award for Excellence in Teaching and the Robert Birkby Teaching Award. Globetti received her Ph.D. from the University of Texas at Austin.

 

Daniel Rice (panelist) is an assistant professor at UNC Law, where he teaches constitutional , First Amendment, and federal Indian law. His recent scholarship explores the interaction between cultural and legal change, the interpretive significance of moral outrage, and the geopolitical foundations of federal Indian law. Rice’s work has appeared in several leading law reviews.

 

Prior to joining academia, Rice clerked for Judge Sri Srinivasan of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, as well as Judge Christopher Cooper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Rice also worked as an attorney at the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection at the Georgetown University Law Center. Rice graduated summa cum laude from the Duke University School of Law. He is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation.

 

Mark Storslee is an associate professor and C. Boyden Gray Distinguished Scholar at UNC Law. His scholarship focuses on constitutional history, religious freedom, and First Amendment law generally.

 

Storslee clerked for Judge Diarmuid O’Scannlain on the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, and later for Associate Justice Neil Gorsuch on the United States Supreme Court. He also previously served as the Executive Director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School. He holds a J.D. from Stanford Law School and a Ph.D. in Religious Studies (ethics) from the University of Virginia.

title: Ackland Film Forum: "Nightcrawler" (Dan Gilroy, 2014)
location: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
description:
Jake Gyllenhaal delivers a career-defining performance as an ambitious freelancer who prowls Los Angeles after dark in search of footage for local television news. The city’s nocturnal landscape of police sirens, flashing lights, and breaking stories becomes the backdrop for a mordant examination of ambition, competition, and media culture in the twenty-first century. 
This film will be introduced by Kino Korner, graduate student association. 
It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. 
UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. 
  
About the Series: 
Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. 
As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. 
From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. 
The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Roots of Discovery: Festival of Lights
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Experience the vibrant traditions of India and explore the connections between cultural heritage, science and the natural world. Celebrate the Festival of Lights through the traditions and stories that have been passed down through generations. Learn how Indian contributions to astronomy, mathematics, medicine and more shaped how people understand the world around us. Join us to discover the ideas that still spark curiosity, creativity and innovation today. 

Presentation
1pm–1:30pm, SECU Daily Planet Theater
Threads of Genius: India’s Legacy in Global Science
From the invention of zero to quantum physics, understanding the genetic code and space exploration, India has continually expanded humanity’s scientific horizon from antiquity to the present. Learn about landmark discoveries and the Indian origin scientists who reshaped global knowledge. 
About the Speaker

Dr. Manisit Das holds a PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences from the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy and works in medical strategy, connecting scientific research with clinical practice and patient outcomes in respiratory diseases. Originally from West Bengal, India, he earned his BSc and MSc in Chemistry at the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur. He has called North Carolina his home for the past decade. 
Activities
Lights from Within 
NC Museum of Natural Sciences
Explore how different animals from the depths of the oceans to the leaves of the forest create light in a process called bioluminescence. Find out how animals use light, often invisible to the human eye, to communicate and find food. 
Poses and Perspectives: The Origin and Evolution of Yoga 
Tarang Mental Health
Yoga originated in Northern India over 5,000 years ago. Learn about the original science and practice of yoga and how it evolved into the modern forms practiced today. 
Kalaatattva: The Elements of Art 
Chani Jain
Indian dance is more than movement — it is a living philosophy where rhythm, expression, and devotion come together to tell timeless stories. Learn about the beauty of Indian dance forms, the philosophy and culture that shape every movement. You’ll go home knowing how to recognize beats and build your own patterns, so that you can dance with ease and confidence. 
Cricket: The Tie that Binds a Billion People
Core Cricket and the Morrisville Raptors
Attitude, energy, enthusiasm and imagination are all you need — besides a bat and a ball. Learn about the sport that has captivated a billion people for over 400 years. 
Painted Traditions: The Story of Henna
Henna Art by Nadia
For thousands of years, henna has adorned hands across North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia to celebrate weddings, holidays and life’s milestones. Discover the roots of this ancient art and see how centuries of tradition come alive in every design.

title: Rethinking Seasonal Cleanup: Why Less Can Be More for Wildlife (in person)
location: Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Are you unsure about when to cut back dormant plants or how many leaves to leave behind? Perhaps you’ve heard about stem-nesting bees or insects that overwinter in fallen foliage and want to support them. Traditional garden practice dictated raking leaves and cutting everything back to “tidy up” before winter. Today, delaying cutbacks and leaving fallen leaves has become more common as gardeners appreciate plants’ unique winter beauty and prioritize wildlife. The best approach depends on your landscape goals and priorities, and this session will help you navigate seasonal cutbacks and leaf management. Join Shannon Currey, education and outreach at Izel Native Plants, to learn strategies that support local wildlife while maintaining a landscape that looks cared for and intentional. This description is for the in-person attendance option—register separately to attend virtually. 
Fee: Free; registration required. 
Parking: Parking fees apply. 
Location: Pelham-Cullen Classroom inside the Barnes Welcome Center. A recording will be shared with all registrants.

title: The AI Election: How Artificial Intelligence Shaped the 2026 Midterms
description:
All Things AI (Live)
One week after Election Day, *Newsweek* will bring together policy experts and Washington insiders to examine the 2026 midterm results through the lens of artificial intelligence.

The discussion will draw on *Newsweek’s* **[AI Policy Scorecard](https://www.newsweek.com/ai-policy-scorecard)**, which tracks the public records of all 537 sitting members of Congress across five areas of AI policy: regulation and governance, data centers and energy, jobs and the economy, safety and privacy, and national security and China.
Using those findings as a starting point, the panel will look at what the results reveal about the emerging politics of AI: where the issue mattered, how positions cut across traditional party lines, and how the composition of the next Congress could reshape the policy fights ahead.

The panel will feature **Nathaniel Persily**, James B. McClatchy professor of law at Stanford Law School and co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative and the Stanford AI Governance Lab; **Brent Buchanan**, founder and CEO of Cygnal; **Nick Penniman**, founder and CEO of Issue One; and **Andrew Mamo**, communications advisor at The Bench.

Moderated by **Gabriel Snyder**, *Newsweek’s* executive editor, enterprise, the conversation will also explore how campaigns and outside groups approached AI during the election, what the results mean for lobbying and advocacy in Washington and which questions are likely to confront lawmakers.

Register here: https://app.sequel.io/newsweek/ai-policy-midterms

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: UNC Postdoctoral Association's Research Cafe
location: Chapel Hill Public Library, Meeting Room A
description:
Have you ever noticed how much hotter a parking lot feels than a tree-lined street on a summer day? Even within the same city, temperatures can vary dramatically over surprisingly short distances. But what causes these differences, and what can we do to make our cities cooler? Cities are often hotter than their rural surroundings, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. As climate change brings rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves, understanding how heat varies within cities is becoming increasingly important.

 

In this talk, Dr. Berk will lead us to explore multitudes of factors that influence urban temperatures, using her findings from right here in Durham and Raleigh. She will also share what we can do about urban heat: from planting trees to installing reflective pavements, which strategies actually work, and how can science help us create cooler, healthier cities.

 

Join us in Chapel Hill Public Library Meeting Room A for this exciting talk! Light refreshment will be provided.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Methods for Conducting Qualitative Coding and Data Analysis
description:
Knowing how to analyze data from qualitative research studies to respond to complex health and social priorities is rewarding, but it can also be daunting. This short course provides students practical skills for coding and analyzing qualitative data for research studies in U.S. and international settings.

 

The short course uses a lab- and discussion-based approach. There will be four modules. In the 1st module, students will learn about the practical steps for qualitative coding and data analysis, including learning about concepts and techniques relating to how to iteratively read narrative data, how to develop codes, how to create a codebook, how to consider hierarchal coding structures, and how to formulate themes from codes. As part of this module, students will also learn about three types of analytical approaches: content analysis, thematic analysis and discourse analysis.

 

In the 2nd module, students will learn about how to use an online qualitative analysis software tool, including how to import a qualitative dataset and codebook and how to assign codes to text. We will review a real-world example of a coded qualitative dataset to discuss techniques for obtaining code extracts, memos, matrices and other analytical tools.

 

In the 3rd module, students will read three qualitative transcripts from a topic selected by the instructor and work in small groups to develop an abbreviated codebook and assign codes to the test transcripts. Students will work in real-time using an online qualitative analysis software. In the final module, students will learn about various ways to present findings from qualitative data analyses. We will critique and discuss various styles for presenting qualitative research, such as using illustrative quotations, visual displays, or quantified qualitative results. Students will learn about the inherent advantages and disadvantages of these styles when presenting their own qualitative findings. This course is designed to provide new knowledge for both introductory and intermediate students.

 

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access.

title: Nov 11 - AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Time, Date and Location**

Nov 11, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-november-11-2026)**

**Agentic RAG: Beyond Retrieve-and-Generate**

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the default pattern for grounding large language models in external knowledge, but most implementations still follow a rigid retrieve-once, generate-once pipeline — one that struggles with multi-hop questions, ambiguous queries, and knowing when its own retrieved context is insufficient. This talk introduces Agentic RAG, where retrieval is treated as an action within an agent's reasoning loop rather than a fixed upstream step.

We'll examine query decomposition and routing for breaking complex questions into targeted sub-queries, self-reflective and corrective retrieval loops that let an agent judge and re-query its own results, and tool-orchestration patterns (via MCP) that let retrieval sit alongside other agent actions like database lookups and API calls. Using a live architecture — evolving a standard RAG chatbot into an agentic, MCP-connected system — we'll walk through what changes in design, and where these systems introduce new failure modes: grounding drift, latency and cost from repeated retrieval loops, and cases where a simpler RAG pipeline still wins.

Attendees will leave with a practical framework for deciding when the added complexity of agentic RAG is worth it, and a set of design patterns for building it correctly.

*About the Speaker*

[Balaji Venkatasubramaniyar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/balaji-venkatasubramaniyar/) is a Technical Lead at Wisdom Infotech, leading a 15+ person engineering team delivering enterprise solutions. With 13+ years of experience in enterprise software and insurance technology, he specializes in agentic AI systems, RAG architectures, and vector databases.

**GeoAI for the Physical World: Earth Observation, Foundation Models, and Urban Digital Twins**

Earth observation provides a unique form of computer vision for understanding the physical world at city to continental scales. In this talk, I will show how satellite imagery, geospatial data, machine learning, and foundation-model representations can be combined to characterize urban environments and environmental conditions.

I will present UrbanScope Open, an open GeoAI digital-twin prototype integrating Earth observation with 3D buildings, vegetation, land-surface temperature, air quality, noise, population, and other urban data. I will also share lessons from my research using geospatial foundation-model embeddings for environmental prediction across Europe.

The talk will discuss how these approaches can contribute to increasingly multimodal AI systems capable of reasoning about real-world environments.

*About the Speaker*

[Cesar Alvarez](https://voxel51.com/events/cesar.alvarez@uni-a.de) is a researcher at the University of Augsburg working at the intersection of GeoAI, Earth observation, remote sensing, and environmental intelligence. His research applies machine learning, computer vision, and geospatial foundation models to problems including urban environments, climate risk, air quality, and agriculture.

**Can agents get curious?**

Most AI agents are good at answering a question once we tell them exactly what to look for. The harder problem is building agents that can explore a complex dataset autonomously: generating hypotheses, deciding which analyses are worth running, allocating additional compute when evidence is ambiguous, and knowing when they have enough evidence to stop.

In this talk, I’ll show an architecture for autonomous research agents that combines structured knowledge, iterative tool use, and explicit evidence tracking to turn open-ended questions into a sequence of testable investigations. I’ll discuss practical lessons from building and evaluating these systems, including why more test-time compute does not automatically produce better research and how provenance and evaluation can make long-running agents more reliable.

I’ll close with a live example of an agent exploring a dataset, revising its hypotheses, and choosing what to investigate next.

*About the Speaker*

[Srivatsa P](https://www.linkedin.com/in/srivatsa-p) is a member of technical staff at Sigma Computing, where he works on AI agents that reason over complex enterprise data. Previously, he worked on machine learning at Apple and conducted research at the MIT Media Lab; outside of traditional ML, he has also worked on mapping coral reefs through underwater imaging, which sparked an enduring interest in how intelligent systems make sense of messy real-world data.

**Does Cross-Validation Work in Deep Learning?**

Cross-validation is a standard in hyperparameter optimization in classical ML, but is generally considered computationally prohibitive and unnecessary in deep learning. We investigated whether CV produces 1. better DL models 2. better estimates of future performance of said models. We focused on medical image classification as an important deep learning application domain.

Our results show that cross-validation consistently and materially reduces the gap between development and independent testing error for relatively small training datasets (up to about 1000 images). The test performance improvement was generally modest. We discuss the implications for deep-learning practitioners, including whether the increased computational cost of cross-validation is justified.

*About the Speaker*

[Ljubomir Buturovic](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ljubomir-buturovic-798156/) is an AI scientist and biotech executive with extensive experience in clinical diagnostics, including work at Inflammatix and Pathwork Diagnostics. His current research focuses on deep-learning image classification, infectious disease adjudication using LLMs, and development of AI models for helping critically ill patients.

title: Business Context in AI Initiatives: Why It Matters More Than You Think
description:
Data Science Raleigh
AI initiatives depend on data—but data without business context can lead to inconsistent answers, unreliable insights, and decisions that miss the mark.

What does “customer,” “revenue,” or even “active” actually mean across your organization? The answer can vary by team, system, or business function.

While these inconsistencies have long created challenges for data and analytics teams, the rise of AI makes the stakes even higher.

In this expert panel, moderated by Jennifer Jackson, Chief Marketing Officer at Actian, we’ll explore why business context has become a critical foundation for trusted AI. Hear perspectives on how organizations can align definitions, metrics, ownership, and relationships across their data environment—and make that context accessible to the AI experiences employees and leaders increasingly rely on.

The session will also feature a live walkthrough demonstrating how modern data platforms can activate business metrics and context with less manual effort, along with practical questions to consider when evaluating whether your data and AI foundation is ready to scale.

**What You'll Learn:**

1️⃣ Why business context matters beyond traditional data and technical teams

2️⃣ How incomplete, inconsistent, or siloed business definitions can impact AI initiatives

3️⃣ How trusted and up-to-date business context can improve the relevance and reliability of AI-driven insights

4️⃣ What it looks like to operationalize business context without creating additional manual overhead

5️⃣ Key questions to ask when evaluating your organization's data and AI readiness

**Who Should Attend**

Business, data, analytics, and technology leaders responsible for developing, scaling, or operationalizing AI initiatives.

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Introduction to Constructivist Grounded Theory
description:
This course introduces participants to constructivist grounded theory (CGT). Grounded theory (GT) methods consist of flexible guidelines to fit particular research problems, not to apply mechanically. With these guidelines, you expedite and systematize data collection and analysis. GT methods can assist researchers in making their work more analytic, precise, and compelling.

In this course, following an exploration of the history and development of GT, we examine GT basic guidelines and major strategies, including initial line-by-line and focused coding, the use of gerunds, memoing, diagramming, theoretical sampling, and categorizing. Throughout the sessions, there is an emphasis on CGT’s epistemological foundation and resultant adaptations to the research process, including regarding the literature review, researcher positionality/ies and reflexivity, and participant involvement.

The course will include a number of hands-on exercises to exemplify, and give participants an opportunity to practice, the strategies being discussed. For the coding exercise, you may bring and use some of your own qualitative data, or if you do not have data yet, some will be supplied. Clear guidelines and support are provided to course participants with regard to all aspects of CGT.

The sessions will utilize CGT readings and resources from Kathy Charmaz, Robert Thornberg, Adele Clarke, and myself, and will draw on the extensive scholarship of Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss. A pack of materials will be shared with participants in advance of the course. This course will be of interest to those doing full CGT studies but also to those who may be interested in learning about and potentially using some of the powerful GT strategies (such as coding) in studies with a different overall methodological approach.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. title: Agent Orchestration in the Enterprise: Coordination, Control, and Scale
description:
Data Science Raleigh
As enterprises move from isolated AI assistants to interconnected agentic systems, orchestration is becoming a critical layer of the AI stack. Coordinating multiple agents across tools, data sources, models, and workflows introduces new opportunities for automation—but also new challenges around reliability, governance, observability, and control.

This session explores what it takes to design and operationalize agent orchestration in enterprise environments. From assigning roles and managing handoffs to monitoring performance and enforcing guardrails, we’ll examine how organizations can build coordinated agent systems that scale without sacrificing trust, security, or human oversight.

**You’ll Learn:**

* From Agents to Systems: How orchestration enables multiple agents, models, tools, and workflows to work together toward shared business objectives.
* Coordination and Handoffs: Approaches for assigning tasks, managing dependencies, resolving conflicts, and maintaining context across agents.
* Control and Observability: How to monitor agent behavior, evaluate performance, and intervene when workflows break down or produce unexpected outcomes.
* Scaling Responsibly: Strategies for governing, securing, and scaling agentic systems while maintaining accountability and appropriate human oversight.

**[Register here](https://datasciconnect.com/events/webinars/agent-orchestration-in-the-enterprise-coordination-control-and-scale/)**

title: Sankai Juku TOTEM: Void and Height
location: Memorial Hall
description:
Sankai Juku creates work that unfolds slowly and deliberately, into what can feel like a new world, where forces like time and gravity seem to act on us in radically new ways.

 

In TOTEM: Void and Height, dancers move with extraordinary presence and precision. Practicing the Japanese dance tradition of Butoh, the company’s performances exist somehow between stillness and action, between gravity and transcendence—and sometimes feel less like watching dance and more like stepping inside a waking dream. 

 

The final work choreographed by their founder Ushio Amagatsu before his death in 2024, TOTEM: Void and Height reflects a lifelong exploration of the relationship between the human body, the natural world, and the forces that shape them both. Through striking imagery and breathtaking physical control, the performance invites audiences to slow down, pay attention, and experience time differently.

 

This is a rare opportunity to encounter one of the world’s most influential contemporary dance companies and the final artistic vision of the artist who shaped it for more than five decades.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/totem/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).
